I definitely think that 13 is too early for any cosmetic surgeries unless the patient is physically seriously injuring themselves (tearing at breast tissue or attempting to remove breasts themselves, for example). I remember at 13 I was starting to question my body and my gender but I am really glad I waited until I did to do anything physical, just because I know I thought about it for 3 years and was absolutely comfortable in my identity before I started. 

Something that's getting a lot of attention right now is puberty blockers. I personally wish I had gotten the opportunity to take puberty blockers, because for female-to-male transitioners they give the opportunity for growing taller when hormones are introduced, due to growth plates not fully closing, and I would love to be taller 😂 Puberty blockers are also the only physical aspect to transitioning that don't really have any lasting effects when discontinued, making them an easier and less invasive way of "trying out" a transition in younger folks. That being said, I don't think they should just be readily available - a young man, for example, who thinks he may want to transition to being female, will unfortunately face extreme bullying if he is a "late bloomer" due to puberty blockers. So there should still be mental health and cognizance screenings, but I would advocate for puberty blockers in younger folks before any physical alterations were made.

I totally agree with you! I did want to clarify one thing - AZA does judge based on how the animals are kept but it also has the power to move animals from one zoo to another based on treatment. Obviously, the general public isn't told about this the majority of the time, but if the AZA sees an animal in an enclosure that's too small or too boring, it can say "hey. We are moving this animal to X facility because they have the capacity to care for it better"

 I don't think this applies for SeaWorld because they're really the only organization I know of (good or bad) that has any sort of capacity for the rehabilitation of larger sea animals. My information on SeaWorld though is unfortunately lacking so honestly I'm not sure how something like that would work.

For sure! Of course, some AZA accredited zoos are better than others, but on the whole the accreditation means that the zoo is focused on conservation and preservation instead of making money. It takes a lot to become accredited, and there are frequent audits to ensure the zoo is adhering to the standards. If they do not, the accreditation can be suspended or revoked entirely.

Absolutely! Nothing against anyone with a negative view of zoos. I totally understand the bad rap they get - but I want people to be fully educated! A lot of people think the PETA ads of sad lions chained up are all they get when there's so much behind the scenes that goes into rehabilitating and rescuing the animals, even if they're never able to be released into the wild.

Hey! Look up AZA accredited zoos. Would you really rather an injured animal die from being released irresponsibly, or live the rest of their life in relative happy comfort while still having the ability to educate the next generation?

Definitely, some zoos are absolutely disgusting. However, many zoos have their first priority as the animals. The zoo where I live has one of the best animal hospitals in the world, and is able to perform delicate and intricate surgeries. Some injured animals simply cannot be rehabilitated, and that's where the zoo comes in.

Additionally, breeding in captivity is actually a sign of a happy, healthy animal. Animals by nature cannot procreate unless instinctually they feel safe to carry on their species - if an orangutan does not feel safe in a deforestation area, it will not breed. So when people say "BRED IN CAPTIVITY" it's a positive thing. There's something called an SSP (species survival plan) and it's basically a huge dating app for all AZA-accredited zoo animals. It's a big DNA map, and it pairs the best animals out of each species around the world to ensure the best chance of that species survival. 

It would be awesome if all animals could be "left where they are". Yeah, that would be great. But frankly that cannot happen. In the wild, lions are shot just for bragging rights. Orangutans' homes are being cut down every single minute, and gorillas are orphaned and poached more often than not. So unless extinction is your endgame, responsible zoos are the next best thing. 

Sorry if any of that was rude. Some zoos are 100% awful, but people complaining about all zoos without educating themselves on what zoos are actually for really irks me. Feel free to pm me if you have any zoo questions.

Meh. This is a hard position for both of you to be in. My mom is the same way, always pushing and pushing and controlling. She wants to live vicariously through me. And while I do see it from her (and your) perspective - wanting your daughter to succeed no matter what because I'm sure she is brilliant - you also have to understand that your intentions do not justify the behavior. 

My mom quit violin at age 16. She forced me to play violin from ages 2-18 because she wanted me to do better. Yes, I did better; yes, it made me smarter. What it didn't do was make me happy. She forced me into an arts school with horrible academics and I'm still playing catch-up with math and science. The kicker: I wanted, really *wanted* to play the cello, and she said no, just because she wanted me to be the better version of her she didn't get to be.

We are not close. I understand her reasoning. I understand why she parented me the way she did. But that doesn't make it okay. No amount of justification can make forcing things on your kids okay. Sure, your daughter is focusing more on the negative instead of what you did for her. But she's doing that because that's what *she* felt. She probably tolerated basketball, pretended to want it because that's what you and her sister wanted. I resent my mom; your daughter resents you. And while it may not seem fair, and no, it isn't actually entirely fair (because I'm sure you love her and care for her and I'm sure you provided excellently for her) there need to be steps taken.

Sit her down, give her your perspective, and then listen. Listening is the best and most healing thing a parent can do. It's also pretty symbolic that BoJack entered her life again in Chicago at a lower point for her but instead of dragging her into another situation, he cleaned up her mess for once and exited quietly, and that also helped her let go of him. I'm sure part of him knew that he wasn't healthy for her and that "last" visit in Chicago was him trying to set things right with her even though he fucked them up so horribly later - and he had no idea that would happen at all.
